The DHT22 (labelled RHT03 in the image) sits in row a of columns 25-28 in pin order VCC, SDA (data), NC, GND. The red wire is in column 25 (VCC to MKR VCC, 3.3 V), the orange wire in column 26 (data to D7), and the black wire in column 28 (GND to MKR GND). Column 27 (NC) is unused.
The 100nF capacitor goes between column 25 (power) and column 28 (GND). The 4.7k pull-up resistor goes between column 25 (power) and column 26 (data). Exact rows b, d and e are read from the image.
The DHT22 is powered from the 3.3 V VCC pin, which is within its 3.3-6 V range.

The microSD card goes in the MKR Zero's built-in slot. The LiPo battery plugs into the MKR Zero's JST BAT connector, so its leads are not wired to individual ports. The USB cable used for programming is not in the parts list, so it is not modelled.
The resistor value is 4.7k (the parts list says 4.75k, the text says 4k7). No electrical edge is added for the DHT22's NC pin.

Fix: I removed the port-specific GND, VCC and A1-A4 edges between mkr1 and shield1. On the shield those ports are screw terminals, which can't join to the MKR board's header pins. The MKR board plugs into the shield's female headers, which the catalogue card doesn't list as ports. So the stack is one port-less 'joined' edge, mkr1 to shield1.
The 5 V vs 3.3 V warning came from the VCC edge I removed. Nothing now puts 5 V on the shield's 3.3 V-rated VCC. The MKR board runs at 3.3 V logic, and the shield's low-power side is 3.3 V.
The tutorial says any MKR family board; I used the MKR WiFi 1010 (arduino-mkr1000-wifi).
The relays are wired inside the shield to MKR pins 1 and 2, so there are no wires for them.

The circuit image was not available, so the LED wiring is my assumption. Pin 3 goes through a jumper wire to LED_1's anode. Its cathode goes through a 220 ohm resistor to the breadboard ground rail. Pin 4 does the same for LED_2. One jumper wire takes MKR GND to the ground rail.
Resistor value (220 ohm) and LED colours are assumed, as the tutorial doesn't give them.
The 24V supply and 24V lamp on the high-power terminals are only an illustrative example, so I did not build them.

Port-kind fixes: the catalogue's Grove cable (grove-cable-4pin-f) has socket-kind ports, which cannot join the carrier's Grove header or the sensor's pins. Pin into pin-hole is a valid pair, and the carrier's A6 Grove connector and the sensor pins are pins.
The carrier's relay terminals are now header-socket kind, so the pump's lead and the USB cable's wire-end are valid joins into them. In reality they are screw terminals that clamp a wire.
The open-ended USB cable's usb-a plug is kind ball, which pairs with the adapter's socket-kind USB-A port (a plug-into-receptacle join). This is a stand-in, because no USB-specific kind exists.

The carrier has a single A6 port for the Grove connector, so the Grove cable's four conductors are shown as one connection from grove1 A1 to carrier A6. The sensor end is wired pin by pin (B1 SIG, B2 NC, B3 VCC, B4 GND).
The pump is wired as the tutorial says: open-ended cable positive to relay 1 NO, pump positive (port 1, the supply side) to relay 1 COM, and the cable negative joined to the pump negative (port 2).
The usb-power-adapter type has only one USB-A port (A), so both USB cables go to port A as a simplification. The tutorial says the adapter has at least 2 USB ports.
Relay 1 is the one used in the circuit text, although the code drives opla.Relay2. The circuit text and image take priority, so relay 1 is wired.
The watering pipe, water container and optional connector strip are left out because they are not electronic parts. No breadboard or jumper wires are used.
Parts are unchanged from step 1.

The schematic image was not visible, so the wiring follows the sketch's pin defines: pin 5 is the white LED, pin 2 is RGB red, pin 3 is RGB blue and pin 4 is RGB green.

[E8] kept on purpose, not a real problem. In the manual's image the red wire runs from the Nano's 3V3 pin to the breadboard + rail, so 3V3 is used as an OUTPUT. The Nano 33 IoT's on-board regulator makes 3.3 V from its USB supply (the board is powered over USB while it runs the sketch and talks to Arduino Cloud). The 4.5 V minimum applies to power fed INTO VIN or VUSB, and nothing here feeds the 3V3 pin. The catalogue card lists 3V3 among the supply pins, which is why the check fires.

I did not move the rail to VUSB (5 V) to quiet the check. That would put a 5 V-powered receiver output on D11, a 3.3 V-only, non-5V-tolerant input, which is a real fault. The manual has no separate supply part (no battery or adapter), so adding one would break the 'exactly the manual's parts' rule.

The IR receiver's legs sit in three neighbouring holes in the card's order GND, VCC, DAT (cols 1, 2, 3 of row e). The black wire goes to GND, the red wire to VCC and the green wire to DAT. This differs slightly from the image, but the nets are the same.

The breadboard has 30 columns in the catalogue, so the image layout (columns 30-63) is compressed to columns 1-27 with the same topology. The lower block of the image is the 't' bank. The Nano straddles the gap, with its bottom row in 't' row e and its top row in 'b' row f.

Nano pin order is inferred. Bottom row, left to right: D1, D0, RST, GND1, D2 to D12. Top row, left to right: VIN, GND, RST, VUSB, A7 to A0, AREF, 3V3, D13. The IR LED, on the anode side through the 330 ohm resistor, goes to D9 and the receiver's DAT goes to D11 (IRrecvDumpV2's default RECV_PIN). Both are read from the image positions.
Only the Nano pins that carry a connection (D9, D11, GND1, 3V3) are listed as joined. The other header pins sit in unused strips.
The sketch, Arduino Cloud Thing and Alexa skill are software, not part of the graph.
